summary.text: A 35-year-old Asian male manual laborer, described as healthy, with no history of smoking, alcohol, intravenous drug misuse, chronic medication use or recent travel, was admitted with five days of tiredness and generalized body pain, more severe in the left upper and lower limbs. He denied fever, cough and chest pain. On admission he had mild generalized edema, muscle tenderness and a swollen, significantly tender left upper limb, with normal heart sounds and no murmur.

Admission laboratory results included creatinine 612 umol/L, creatine kinase 1269 U/L, myoglobin 4284 ng/mL and C-reactive protein 340 mg/L, with high anion gap metabolic acidosis, microscopic hematuria and negative HIV, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, respiratory virus and COVID-19 screening. A provisional diagnosis of rhabdomyolysis with acute kidney injury was made, with intravenous hydration and nephrology consultation. Echocardiography showed severe mitral regurgitation, and a blood culture revealed S. dysgalactiae sensitive to ceftriaxone.

Transesophageal echocardiography showed a mobile echogenic mass on the anterior and posterior mitral leaflets, and infective endocarditis was diagnosed. MRI of the left upper limb showed multiple small abscesses and features suggestive of necrotizing fasciitis; no surgical procedure was performed. He was treated with ceftriaxone, the repeat blood culture was negative five days after starting antibiotics, and blood urea and serum creatinine returned to normal on day 10. In the third week he developed left wrist pain and swelling, and arthrotomy with tissue biopsy on day 29 indicated reactive arthritis without pus.

He was discharged home 35 days after being hospitalized and received IV antibiotic for an additional 10 days. At the clinic three weeks following discharge he was symptom-free except for slight left wrist pain, with normal functional ability and laboratory results. Valve replacement surgery was planned for a later stage, but he chose to have it in his home country.
